lines.text: Stone spheres in the jungle, coffee on the hills, and a nation that chose to have no army. This is the story of Costa Rica.
Some three thousand years ago, people began building at Guayabo, a town that grew to have paved roads and aqueducts to carry water.
In the south, the Diquis people carved hundreds of stone balls, some almost perfectly round. Why they made them is still a mystery.
Spain's colony here was poor and remote. In 1736 a small settlement was founded in the central valley, today's capital, San Jose.
In 1821 Costa Rica became free of Spain, and coffee growing on its hills soon made it prosper.
Freedom came with the Act of Independence of the fifteenth of September 1821, which freed all of Central America from Spain.
In the 1850s an American adventurer, William Walker, tried to rule the region. Costa Rica joined its neighbours and drove him out.
Jose Figueres Ferrer would lead the country three times, and make the boldest choice in its history.
Oscar Arias would become president and win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987, for a plan to bring peace to Central America.
After a short civil war in 1948, Figueres abolished the army, a choice that has held ever since.
Rodrigo Chaves Robles, an economist, would become president in 2022.
In a small cloud forest lived a bright orange toad, found nowhere else. Last seen in 1989, it became a warning of how fragile nature is.
That forest, Monteverde, was protected as a reserve in 1972, and Costa Rica became known around the world for its green, living forests.
And Keylor Navas, a goalkeeper from Costa Rica, would win three Champions League titles with Real Madrid.
A small country without an army, Costa Rica found its strength in peace and in its forests.
